title: Why your skin is exhausted by your 10-step routine - South China Morning Post
text:
Why minimalist skincare is replacing the 10-step routine | South China Morning Post Latest Luxury Fashion Beauty People Lifestyle Buy Style Trends Why your skin is exhausted by your 10-step routine Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Trends Why minimalist skincare is replacing the 10-step routine 
 STORY Carolina Malis Nov 7, 2026 Hailey Bieber holds a bottle of the Rhode Peptide Glazing Fluid. Photo: Handout
 Beauty + FOLLOW Dermatologists explain why stacking active ingredients does more harm than good – and how returning to a simple cleanser, moisturiser and SPF restores the skin barrier
 Some time in the last decade the bathroom shelf turned into a filing system. A cleanser for the morning and a different one for the evening ; an acid on Tuesday, a retinol on Wednesday – and a barrier cream for the two nights afterwards, while your face recovers from the first two. But at some point, people started getting tired. Not of skincare exactly, but more of the admin: the cross-referencing, the percentages; the low-grade sense that there’s a step you’ve missed and a launch you haven’t caught up with. The 10-step Korean routine landed in the West around 2015. What travelled best was the number – that being the part that’s easiest to translate and the part that sells. Korea had moved on again by the early 2020s into “skip-care”, whereby repetitive steps are cut in favour of formulas doing more than one job . KraveBeauty, founded by South Korean beauty YouTuber Liah Yoo, built a whole brand position around the idea of pressing reset, on the basis that a 10-product routine is a lot to ask of anyone’s evening, never mind their skin. KraveBeauty products. Photo: Handout Advertisement “Overloading the skin with multiple products with multiple active ingredients can cause more harm than good,” says Dr Nihull Jakharia-Shah, consultant dermatologist at the Medical Chambers Kensington, in London. “It can lead to irritation and sensitisation , which is not the desired goal of any skincare regime.” Sensitisation is the point at which skin that used to tolerate something stops doing so – occasionally, for good. Additionally, once you’re eight layers deep, “the products battle for contact with the skin to be absorbed or elicit their active effect”, Jakharia-Shah notes. Some of what you’ve applied is essentially sitting on top of the rest of it, doing very little. So the actual bare minimum is refreshingly short. “A gentle cleanser; a bland, fragrance-free emollient, and SPF applied throughout the day ,” Jakharia-Shah advises. “That’s the foundation of any skincare routine and all that’s needed for someone with otherwise healthy skin.” Everything past those three is a decision rather than the default.
